evidence.excerpt: When a contract electronics assembler takes on new product variants, inspection workload changes in ways that are difficult to predict from capacity calculations alone because defect rates, test durations, and re-test probabilities vary across variants. This paper describes a discrete-event simulation model of a three-stage inspection process (automated optical inspection, in-circuit test, functional test) calibrated with empirical process time distributions and per-variant defect rates collected over 12 months. The model is used to evaluate quality cost implications of four product-mix scenarios representing different ratios of high-complexity to standard-complexity boards. Results show that appraisal cost per good unit increases nonlinearly above a complexity ratio of approximately 0.45 due to bottleneck formation at functional test. Under the highest complexity scenario, total quality cost per unit is 23% above the baseline, with 71% of the increase attributable to internal failure costs generated by inspection queue-induced rework batching. The paper uses the simulation output to recommend a staffing and inspection sequencing policy that reduces this cost penalty to 11%.
